paragraphs: Rain had washed the blood from Wei Bridge once, but dark red marks still soaked the cracks between its planks. On the southern bank, a shelter of thatch had been put up. Military clerks laid out the wooden name tablets recovered from the fighting, recording each by company, squad, and the hour at which it had been found. On the reverse of each tablet belonging to an unknown soldier they cut a small circle. The carving knife was blunt. By evening, the clerk’s thumb had blistered.

Fu Shao came to claim something. It was a leather armguard, with a copper coin sewn into its lining, stiffened by blood. The clerk assumed he was recovering it for a man of his own unit and lifted his brush to ask the name. Fu Shao said it belonged to Fu En, from the north side of the bridge. The brush hovered above the page. “Do we enter the enemy’s belongings too?” the clerk asked.
“He once saved my life.”

The clerk looked at him, turned to another page, and wrote Fu En’s name. Fu Shao took the armguard and left the shelter with his head bowed. The new Qin banner at the bridgehead clung to its pole beneath the rain. Layer after layer of wet silk hung down, and it was impossible to imagine how vast it had appeared when the wind spread it on the day of battle.
Three batches of petitions demanding Fu Luo’s execution had already reached the palace gates of Chang’an.

The first came from court officials, written neatly and signed by more than seventy men. The second was from the soldiers who had fought at Wei Bridge. It bore only the private seals of twelve commandants and asked a single question: When a common soldier disobeys orders, he pays with his life; when a prince does so, is a reprimand enough? The third petition contained no formal words at all. Families of those who had died in the night fires stood outside the southern gate carrying wooden ancestral tablets. Some held a clay basin burned through on one side; others clutched a little jacket that would never again be worn. When rain began, they hid the tablets in their sleeves and left themselves exposed.

Fu Jian looked down from the palace wall. At the front of the crowd stood an old man with snow-white hair who refused to kneel. He held a memorial tablet so tightly that his knuckles had turned blue. A guard told him to move under the eaves out of the rain. The old man asked only, “Who, exactly, is the Heavenly King going to kill?”
Fu Jian heard him clearly, but he could not answer from behind the palace wall.

That night Fu Hong brought the files of the Court of the Imperial Clan. Their edges were worn with handling. Father and son studied them by lamplight until the water clock ran out. Fu Luo admitted that he had personally ordered the crossing at Wei Bridge. He admitted detaining the messengers and concealing the true circumstances of Chang Xuan’s death; he acknowledged that he had doubted the secret edict calling for a purge of the court. But the testimony about the crossbowmen who killed Chang Xuan, the change-of-guard order at Zhangcheng Gate, and the fires contradicted itself. One witness accused a secretary from Fu Luo’s residence of passing a secret note; the secretary maintained that he had not left the residence that night. The note was missing, and the groom who had carried the message was dead.
“And the two edicts your uncle brought back?” Fu Jian asked.

“Both the genuine and the false edict are sealed in the Secretariat. Separate samples of the seal paste have been taken.” Fu Hong pushed over a thin register. “East Pass has sent three scribes under guard. One claims to recognize the paper; another knows the courier; the third acknowledges nothing. The Judicial Commandant will check the watches they describe before proceeding.”

Fu Jian opened a slip of paper tucked inside the register. His imperial name had been copied upon it with remarkable skill. Without knowing where it came from, he might not have detected the forgery at first glance himself.
“Who does Fu Luo say brought it?”
“He says he does not know the man who delivered the edict.”
“Do you believe him?”

Fu Hong pressed his lips together. “I don’t know. But he knew there was something wrong with the edict and still ordered copies sent to his camps. There are witnesses to that, and his own confession.”

Fu Jian put the slip down. Another register lay on the desk, listing the killed and wounded. Beside the name of a granary guard, the handwriting suddenly grew uneven, as though the scribe’s hand had been shaking when he wrote. Fu Jian asked his son, “You saw the night fires with your own eyes. Did you want Fu Luo dead?”
“I did.”
“And now?”

“At Wei Bridge, I wanted him dead then too.” Fu Hong looked down at the fresh scabs on his palms; whenever he made a fist, the skin pulled tight. “But I went to the Court of the Imperial Clan and saw him sitting in his cell. It struck me that some of the men I hate most are not named anywhere in the charge sheet. Those who set the fires had hands of their own. Those who forged the edicts had their own brushes. Fu Luo brought an army to Chang’an. He cannot escape that. For the other crimes, we must go on asking questions.”

For a long time Fu Jian said nothing. Outside the window rain ran down the roof channels, sounding like a multitude of small footsteps. He picked up the vermilion brush and wrote two lines upon a blank sheet: QUESTION THE CASES SEPARATELY. WITNESS TESTIMONY AND PHYSICAL EVIDENCE SHALL NOT BE USED AS SUBSTITUTES FOR ONE ANOTHER. He set down the brush.

At court the next day, Murong Chui urged capital punishment under military law. He made no argument from Chang Xuan’s death or from the night fires. He spoke only of Wei Bridge. “The Duke of Beihai saw the Heavenly King’s banner and sounded the horns to advance across the bridge. Those who died on the north bank and those who died on the south were all men upon the court’s military rolls. If this offense is lightly forgiven, every man with an army will remember that bridge.”
Someone among the Fu clansmen sneered, “How thoughtful of the Champion General to concern himself with the affairs of our Fu family.”

Murong did not answer the insult. He took a page from the register of wounded soldiers and handed it to the man. Several names belonged to Xianbei soldiers and several to Di. The last was a boy of seventeen who had lost his left arm. The clansman’s face darkened as he read.

Yao Chang also called for severe punishment of the chief offender. He spoke gently, as though helping the court find a path through the crisis: it was right to distinguish those forced to follow from those who did so willingly, but princes and commanders who took up arms first must not be allowed to push the blame upon their men. As Fu Jian listened, he remembered Yao rescuing the imperial granary during the fires and the missing paper from the Right Guard’s inner treasury. He held both facts before him and allowed neither to erase the other.

At dusk Fu Rong at last returned from Anding. Without even shaking the dust from his armor, he presented the staff of authority, the half-tally, and the list of witnesses sealed at East Pass. He did not sit down. He stood near the hall entrance while the ministers debated for almost half an hour. When he spoke, it was to ask, “Of the thirty thousand former followers of Fu Luo, how many are still at home? How many died? How many were brought along to Chang’an against their will?”
“The figures are being checked,” Quan Yi answered.

“Then identify the living first,” Fu Rong said. “Several towns in Beidi are still shutting their gates against new officials. If we issue an order tonight to execute every rebel, tomorrow those people will have no choice but to become rebels in truth.”
Another minister asked, “What of the private soldiers of the imperial clan? Surely we cannot let them remain.”

Quan Yi had several chests of records brought forward. Old household retinues, armed estate guards, pasture horsemen—the categories differed, but the same name appeared again and again across their pages. Fu Rong opened one volume at random and pointed out a cavalryman whose name had been struck from the Beidi army’s rolls but who still received grain as a guard at a prince’s residence. Fu Jian considered the record, had the volume sealed apart, and ordered the discussion postponed until after the court had dispersed.

“Tonight we are judging Fu Luo’s crimes,” he said. “The old practice of granting military commands to imperial kinsmen must be dealt with separately. Both matters are grave. Neither should be allowed to hide the shame of the other.”
On the tenth day of Fu Luo’s confinement, Fu Jian visited the Court of the Imperial Clan.

The underground cell smelled of mildew. A clay bowl stood in the corner, bits of candle wax floating upon its water. Fu Luo wore no heavy cangue, but his wrists were rubbed raw by iron chains. He was laying shards of broken pottery in a row beside the wall. Fu Jian looked and asked what they represented.
“The men on the bridge.”
“Can you count them all?”
“No.”
“Then why keep laying them out?”

Fu Luo nudged one crooked fragment straight with his foot before looking up. “When I commanded men in Beidi and one died, I knew his name and what he had left at home. More men died on the bridge than I ever knew.”
“You could still have kept them from dying.”

Fu Luo’s face tightened. After a long silence he said, “Your Majesty told me to surrender my army on the bridge. If I had surrendered, I would have faced trial that very night. It wasn’t the Judicial Commandant I feared. I feared that afterward, whenever anyone mentioned Beidi, Your Majesty would not even want to hear my name.”
“So you sent them onto the bridge?”
“Yes.”
His answer was almost inaudible. The defense that had once seemed as hard as iron had dwindled to a single word.

Fu Jian studied him. In their youth they had shared the same brazier outside a tent through the long nights of Guanzhong. Once Fu Luo had been unable to sleep because of chilblains and had told a clumsy joke in hopes of making his elder brother laugh. Now, across the dim lamp in the prison, Fu Jian could scarcely find any part of that boy in the thin face before him.
“Who killed Chang Xuan?”
“I never ordered him killed.”
“You falsely reported that cavalry from Dai had ambushed him.”
“I was afraid that if I told the truth, every soldier in Beidi would be taken from me.”
“Who set the fires in Chang’an?”
“I don’t know.”
“And the man who brought the false edict?”
Fu Luo watched the candle flame. “He delivered a way out of my troubles, and he delivered the rope for my neck. If I knew who he was, I might not spare him.”

He did not sound as though he were lying. Yet Fu Jian did not write the word innocent beside his name, even in his own mind. As he turned to leave, Fu Luo suddenly asked, “Your Majesty, is there anyone left to speak for me?”
“Yes.”
“Who?”
“The greatest number are those asking for your death.”
Fu Luo lowered his eyes. After a moment he laughed. Fu Jian left the cell and heard the laughter break and fade along the passage behind him.

The final hearing was held in a government hall outside the southern gate. A wooden awning was erected in the outer yard, so that bereaved families could enter according to the registers and listen. Feathered Guard soldiers held open a narrow path. Hundreds were waiting by the roadside before daylight: some carried white mourning banners, others had traveled a thousand li from Beidi in search of a son’s name. The chief judge, from the Court of the Imperial Clan, first recited the charges of unlawful recruitment, detention of imperial messengers, armed advance upon the capital, and attack in defiance of an edict at Wei Bridge. He then announced that the Judicial Commandant had not yet found direct orders linking Fu Luo to the night fires or the murder of Chang Xuan; those investigations would continue separately.

Angry cries rose at once beyond the awning. Some accused the officials of eating the Fu family’s grain and not daring to execute one of its own. Others asked whether the eleven guards killed with Chang Xuan had died for nothing. Fu Rong stood behind the listeners without a sword at his waist, but his fingers were white around the staff of authority he held.

Witnesses came forward one at a time. Surviving guards recognized the boots of the men who had ambushed them, but could not identify their faces. A Beidi officer admitted marching south with Fu Luo and hearing the signal to advance at Wei Bridge, yet claimed that even as the horns sounded he had hoped they were only meant as a threat. Fu Luo listened without interrupting. When someone described the northern supervising troops shooting their own men who tried to surrender, he jerked his head up. Asked whether he knew the positions of those troops, he said yes, but could not name the individual archers.

Chen Mu’s father was admitted to the awning in the afternoon. He wore hemp clothes washed nearly white and carried his son’s charred military name tablet against his chest. Chen Mu had guarded the imperial granary and died outside it on the night of the fires. The old man knew none of the courtesies of a courtroom. He took one step forward and dropped to his knees. As he spoke, his voice rose sharply. “My son was always afraid of fire. Even when he tended the stove at home, he used long chopsticks. That night they told him to guard the granary, and he went. Now a man who ordered thirty thousand soldiers to march on the capital says he never told anyone to start a fire, and that’s enough to clear him?”
No one answered him at once. The old man caught his breath, then asked Fu Luo on the raised platform, “Duke of Beihai, is your son still alive?”
Fu Luo’s lips moved, but he made no reply.
“Mine is gone.” The old man laid the tablet upon the ground as gently as though he feared it might still feel pain.

The Judicial Commandant then read the findings of the separate investigation. Several men who had ignited the haystacks on the southern side of the imperial granary had been identified; whose orders they had followed remained unknown. The crowd was still dissatisfied. That day, no matter how many case files were read, grief kept rising in broken cries beneath the awning, drowning the clerks' voices again and again.

By late afternoon the officials of the Court of the Imperial Clan had agreed to recommend the supreme penalty against Fu Luo. Fu Jian sat high above them for a long time. The Secretariat brought the judgment for imperial confirmation. His vermilion brush lay at hand. He touched it with his fingers but did not lift it.

Murong Chui watched him, knowing that this decision was harder than the battle at Wei Bridge. If Fu Luo died, his former troops in Beidi might still refuse to accept the court. If he lived, the families of the dead would ask whether there were two kinds of law beneath heaven. Fu Jian understood that whichever word he wrote, others would invent hidden motives for it.

At last, he wrote an edict commuting the death sentence. Fu Luo was found guilty, stripped of rank, removed from the imperial clan’s official rolls, and deprived of his fief and the revenues of his former retainers. He was to remain confined for life in a detached palace, receiving no guests and holding no troops. Officers implicated in the affair would be judged separately according to the evidence against each. Fu Jian made no attempt to present this as the inevitable result of legal procedure. At the end of the edict he declared openly that he, the Heavenly King, had personally remitted a sentence of death, and that he alone would answer for objections.

An uproar shook the yard. Some cursed, some wept, and some quietly breathed easier. Chen Mu’s father was still on his knees. After a long time he struggled to his feet. He offered neither thanks nor cries of long life. He picked up the name tablet and walked away along the narrow gap opened through the crowd.

Fu Hong followed him to the gate. Seeing how unsteady the old man’s steps were, he ordered someone to support him. The man waved the offer away. He asked only, “Can my son’s death benefit go to his mother? She has lost her sight. She went to the granary office several times, and nobody would acknowledge her claim.”
Fu Hong wrote the words in the empty margin of the case file. He had learned to read what a document contained; only now did he begin to understand how many people were missing from its pages.

Three days after the judgment, a separate edict reorganizing the military registers was issued by the Secretariat. Fiefs of imperial kinsmen were forbidden to maintain armed battalions of their own. Every former household guard was to be registered individually. Those wishing to remain soldiers would transfer to the state army; those wishing to farm would surrender their weapons and return to their homes. Unarmed servants retained by each household would be limited according to the size of the residence, and private military signals were prohibited. Emergency recruitment on the frontier remained possible, but each levy had to be reported promptly. The censors began their inspection with the imperial clan’s estates near the capital. By that evening one pasture northwest of Chang’an stood empty, with only severed reins left hanging in the horse pens.
Someone held up the edict and asked Fu Rong, “Fu Luo’s punishment has been decided. Why are you now pursuing members of the imperial clan who never rebelled?”

Fu Rong did not call it punishment. He handed the questioner a list. It showed three men who had died at Wei Bridge still drawing grain from two princely residences. The man stared at it for a long time, then snapped the register shut in anger, still unwilling to accept what it meant. Fu Rong told him to take it home and examine the grain accounts of his own household more carefully.

On the morning Fu Luo was sent to the detached palace, the clouds hung low. The carriage wheels rolled through wet mud without the bronze bells of a prison wagon. Fu Jian waited alone outside the palace gate. The escort soldiers stepped back to let these two men—sovereign and subject, who had once shared a fire as boys—speak a few last words.
Fu Luo wore a coarse cloth robe. The wounds from the iron fetters had darkened into scabs around his wrists. His first question was, “Are the soldiers in Beidi still there?”
“Some have been discharged, some remain on the frontier. Someone must keep watch at the beacons.”
“Who commands them?”
“A newly appointed general.”
Fu Luo gave a quiet laugh. “So my Beidi still needs someone to defend it.”
“Beidi never belonged to you alone.”

Fu Luo looked up as though about to argue. Instead he pulled his sleeves lower over his wrists. Before stepping into the carriage, he turned back suddenly. “On the night of the spring banquet, if Your Majesty had let me sit at the feast instead of leaving that empty place for Murong Chui, would things have been different?”
Fu Jian looked at the carriage shaft. After a long while he said, “Perhaps. But that empty seat cannot answer for what you chose to do afterward.”
“I know.”

Silence settled within the carriage. Fu Luo turned toward the city. He knew those rooftops well. In former days whenever he came to the palace, through spring snow or autumn rain, someone had always raised the curtain at its gate for him before he reached it.
“Yao Chang once asked me,” he said, his voice fading, “whether Your Majesty would still listen to me on the day I no longer commanded an army.”
“I am listening to you now.”
“I hear you.” Fu Luo looked at him. “But we were both a step too late.”

He sat back. The carriage pole creaked and the horses moved slowly away. Fu Jian did not watch until they vanished. As the carriage rounded a street corner, a child called out in the distance, selling fresh fish caught at Wei Bridge. So many had died there, yet the Wei kept flowing, and people still cast their nets. Fu Jian stood in the cold wind and found the child’s voice harder to bear than all the curses he had heard outside the southern gate.

That evening, in camp, Fu Shao handed Fu En’s armguard to an old veteran of their former unit who had come to claim the dead man’s belongings. The soldier found the copper coin still sewn inside. His nose stung. “The court didn’t leave him lying beside the bridge like a common bandit, did it?”
“He was buried,” Fu Shao said.
“Who buried him?”
“We did.”

The veteran closed his fist around the armguard and bowed deeply after a long silence. Fu Shao did not return the bow. He looked at the rows of shields washed clean and stacked through the camp, remembering that drills would begin again tomorrow. Nothing they could practice would teach them to forget what had happened on the bridge.
